description: This is my first NASA Space Apps Challenge, and I’m excited to build something fun and useful with NASA data.
summary: Ghost Rovers is an interactive web experience that lets students meet the machines NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Nine spacecraft, including Apollo 11 Eagle, Surveyor 3, the Apollo 17 rover, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10 and Voyager 1, each tell their own story in the first person: why they were sent, what they discovered and how their missions ended. Users tap a glowing dot on a map, spin a 3D model of the machine, and read its story. It turns dense mission histories into a personal story for school-age and casual space fans, so they can feel connected to these robotic explorers and the science they made possible.
details:
Ghost Rovers is a story-driven web page about hardware left behind on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. A map shows nine machines as dots: blue pulsing dots are still working, silver dots have gone quiet. Choosing a machine opens a 3D model that can be dragged and zoomed, and a short story in its own voice with three parts: "In my own words", "What I discovered" and "Last heard". After meeting all nine, a closing message links the machines to NASA's return to the Moon with the Artemis program.

The page is a single HTML file that runs in any browser with no download or account. It uses Three.js to show simple 3D models built from basic shapes, and users can load their own .glb model of a machine, for example one from NASA's 3D Resources. The stories are written from NASA mission records. Where an exact fact matters, such as how far Apollo 12 landed from Surveyor 3, we checked it against NASA pages and corrected our text.

Students hear mostly about active missions. This project gives silent machines a voice, which makes history and engineering easier and more fun to understand. It works on phones and computers, and it is easy to extend with more machines.

I want students to feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers and to see how each mission answered real scientific questions about water, soil, dust, distance and the Moon's slow drift away from Earth.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js (3D), the Inter typeface, and Claude (Anthropic), which we used to help build it.
